To run the example yourself, follow the notebook quickstart.

Simulate parallel trajectories for adenylate kinase¶

This notebook loads adenylate kinase from the PDB, samples a starting structure, then propagates several independent trajectories from that structure.

[!NOTE] Here each mdtraj.Trajectory is a time-ordered rollout, unlike the unordered bag of samples stored in mdtraj.Trajectory by other BioEmu2 sampling APIs.

For other propagation workflows, see the propagation guide.

For installation and hardware requirements, see the notebook quickstart.

In [1]:
from pathlib import Path

import mdtraj
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from bioemu2 import (
    System,
    load_model,
    sample_equilibrium,
    save_frames,
    simulate_trajectory,
)
from bioemu2.visualization import view_trajectory

Prepare the system and model¶

In [2]:
system = System.from_pdb_id("1AKE")
model = load_model()

Sample a starting conformation¶

In [3]:
x0: mdtraj.Trajectory = sample_equilibrium(
    system,
    model=model,
    num_samples=1,
    batch_size=1,
    seed=0,
)

Propagate¶

Repeat the initial conformation once for each independent trajectory. simulate_trajectory() computes one embedding, reuses it across every step, and returns one time-ordered trajectory per starting frame. Each trajectory includes the starting structure at time zero and one frame per propagation step.

In [4]:
lag_time_ns = 50
num_trajectory_steps = 20
num_trajectories = 4

trajectories = simulate_trajectory(
    system,
    model=model,
    x0=x0[[0] * num_trajectories],
    lag_time_ns=lag_time_ns,
    num_trajectory_steps=num_trajectory_steps,
    seed=1,
)
print(
    f"Generated {len(trajectories)} trajectories with "
    f"{trajectories[0].n_frames} frames each."
)

Generated 4 trajectories with 21 frames each.

Visualize the propagated trajectory¶

Each endpoint is aligned to its own previous frame. Animate the first trajectory; the distance plot below shows all trajectories.

In [5]:
view = view_trajectory(trajectories[0])
view.show()

3Dmol.js failed to load for some reason. Please check your browser console for error messages.

Save the propagated trajectory¶

In [6]:
output_dir = Path("outputs/simulate_a_trajectory")
for i, trajectory in enumerate(trajectories, start=1):
    output_path = save_frames(trajectory, output_dir / f"trajectory_{i:02d}")
    print(f"saved trajectory {i} to {output_path}")

saved trajectory 1 to outputs/simulate_a_trajectory/trajectory_01/samples.xtc
saved trajectory 2 to outputs/simulate_a_trajectory/trajectory_02/samples.xtc
saved trajectory 3 to outputs/simulate_a_trajectory/trajectory_03/samples.xtc
saved trajectory 4 to outputs/simulate_a_trajectory/trajectory_04/samples.xtc

Compare the trajectories¶

Plot the distance between the alpha carbons of residues 35 and 125 (1-based topology order). These residues lie in the NMP and LID domains, which move relative to each other as adenylate kinase opens and closes. Each line follows one trajectory across all propagation steps. MDTraj stores frame times in picoseconds; divide by 1000 to plot elapsed time in nanoseconds.

In [7]:
ca35 = system.topology.residue(34).atom("CA")
ca125 = system.topology.residue(124).atom("CA")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for i, trajectory in enumerate(trajectories, start=1):
    times_ns = trajectory.time / 1000
    distance_nm = mdtraj.compute_distances(trajectory, [[ca35.index, ca125.index]])[:, 0]
    ax.plot(times_ns, distance_nm, marker="o", markersize=3, label=f"Trajectory {i}")
ax.set(xlabel="Elapsed time (ns)", ylabel="CA 35-CA 125 distance (nm)")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(output_dir / "ca_distance.png", dpi=160)
plt.show()
